title: Fake university email
fromReveal: Full sender address: futa-student-support@gmail.com (a free Gmail account, not a university domain)
subject: URGENT: Portal account suspension
body: Your portal account will be SUSPENDED within 24 hours because of a system upgrade. To avoid losing your course registration, verify your account now by entering your matric number and password.
linkReveal: This link would go to: http://futa-portal-verify.example/login (fictional, not clickable)

indicators.t: Sender uses a free Gmail address, not an official university address
indicators.why: Organisations normally send from their own domain. Anyone can create a Gmail address with 'FUTA' in the name.
Urgency and threats push you to act before you think. This is a classic pressure tactic.

indicators.t: Asks you to enter your password through a link
indicators.why: Genuine services do not ask you to re-enter your password because of an 'upgrade'.

indicators.t: The link destination does not match the official portal
indicators.why: Inspect a link before trusting it. Look at the real address, not the button text.
Mass messages are often generic. On its own this is weak evidence, but it adds up with the other signs.

indicators.t: The message mentions the university's name
indicators.why: Using a real name proves nothing. Scammers copy names, tone and logos freely.

actions.t: Click the link quickly so my account is not suspended
actions.why: Acting under pressure is exactly what the sender wants.

actions.t: Reply with my matric number to ask if it is real
actions.why: Replying confirms your address is active and shares details with a stranger.

actions.t: Do not click. Open the official portal by typing its address yourself, or ask the ICT office, then report the email
actions.why: Verifying through an independent, official channel is the safest response.

actions.t: Forward it to coursemates so they can verify too
actions.why: Forwarding spreads the scam. Warn people, but do not pass on the link.

title: Fake scholarship WhatsApp message
fromReveal: Unknown number, not saved in your contacts, with no verifiable organisation behind it.
body: 🎓 CONGRATULATIONS! You have been selected for a ₦150,000 Student Support Scholarship!
To receive your award, pay a ₦5,000 registration fee and send your full name, ID number and account number. Only 50 slots left! Forward to 10 groups.
linkReveal: This link would go to: http://student-grants-ng.example/apply (fictional, not clickable)

indicators.t: Asks for a ₦5,000 fee before you receive anything
indicators.why: Paying a fee to unlock a prize or grant is the hallmark of advance-fee fraud.

indicators.t: Promises a large reward for no application or merit
indicators.why: Real scholarships involve applications, eligibility criteria and selection. You cannot be 'selected' for something you never applied for.
These details can be used for identity theft or to access your money.

indicators.t: Pressure: 'only 50 slots left' and 'forward to 10 groups'
indicators.why: Scarcity and viral forwarding are used to stop you from checking.

indicators.t: No named awarding body or official website
indicators.why: Genuine scholarships name the provider, and you can confirm them on the provider's official site.

indicators.t: The message uses a friendly, excited tone
indicators.why: Tone is not evidence. Friendly messages can be fraudulent and serious ones can be genuine.

actions.t: Pay the ₦5,000. It is small compared with ₦150,000
actions.why: The fee is the scam. Victims rarely get anything back.

actions.t: Send only my name to see what happens
actions.why: Even small details help scammers target you further.

actions.t: Forward it to my groups so friends do not miss out
actions.why: You would be spreading a scam to people who trust you.

actions.t: Do not respond. Check the scholarship provider's official website or the student affairs office, and report or block the number
actions.why: Checking official sources is how you separate real opportunities from fraud.

title: Fake bank alert
fromReveal: Sender names can be faked. An SMS sender name is not proof that the bank sent the message.
body: Unity Trust Bank (fictional): Your account has been restricted due to unusual activity. Restore access within 2 hours or it will be closed.
Log in to confirm your details:
linkReveal: This link would go to: http://unitytrust-secure-login.example/restore (fictional look-alike address, not clickable)

indicators.t: The web address is not the bank's official domain
indicators.why: Look-alike addresses are used to impersonate banks and harvest your login details.
Real banks do not close accounts on a two-hour countdown by text.

indicators.t: Asks you to log in via a link to confirm details
indicators.why: This is credential harvesting: the fake page records whatever you type.

indicators.t: Generic message with no personal details
indicators.why: It does not mention your name or any real account details, so it could be sent to thousands of people.

indicators.t: The message arrived as an SMS
indicators.why: Banks do send genuine SMS alerts. The channel alone is not the problem. The link and the pressure are.
Naming a bank is cheap. Impersonation relies on it.

actions.t: Tap the link and log in to check what is wrong
actions.why: A fake login page would capture your username and password.

actions.t: Do not use the link. Open the bank's official app or call the number on your card or the official website
actions.why: Using channels you already trust avoids the trap entirely.
Replying can confirm your number is active and invite more messages.

actions.t: Send the OTP when they call to help me
actions.why: Never share OTPs or PINs with anyone, including people claiming to be the bank.
